title: The Event Loop
tagline: The runtime model behind every interview puzzle: stack, queues, microtasks, and when the browser actually paints.

lessons.title: The Runtime Model: Stack, Heap, Queues
lessons.body:
# The Runtime Model: Stack, Heap, Queues

JavaScript itself is single-threaded. Concurrency comes from the *runtime* — the browser or Node — which owns the event loop. The model has four parts; interviews expect you to name all four and say what each does.

## The four parts

- **Call stack** — where your code runs. Function calls push frames; returns pop them. LIFO, fixed size: unbounded recursion throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`.
- **Heap** — where objects live. Unstructured memory; allocation and GC happen here.
- **Task queue** (macrotask queue) — callbacks waiting their turn: `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, I/O completions, UI events.
- **Microtask queue** — higher-priority callbacks: promise reactions, `queueMicrotask`, `MutationObserver`.

## The loop, precisely

1. Execute the current task (initially, the whole script) until the call stack is empty — **run to completion**: a running task is never preempted by another task.
2. Drain the microtask queue completely (jobs queued *during* the drain also run now).
3. Optionally render (browsers — next lesson).
4. Dequeue the next macrotask and go to 1.

Web APIs (`setTimeout`, `fetch`, DOM listeners) live *outside* the JS engine. Calling `setTimeout(cb, 0)` doesn't run anything — it asks the runtime to enqueue `cb` as a macrotask after ~0ms. The callback still waits behind everything already queued.

```js
console.log('script start');
setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'), 0);
console.log('script end');
// 'script start', 'script end', 'timeout'
// The timeout callback waits: the current task must finish first.
```

## Why this matters in production

A `while` loop that runs 3 seconds doesn't "use a thread" — it *is* the thread. Timers don't fire, clicks don't register, fetch callbacks don't run, and the page doesn't paint until it finishes. Every main-thread performance bug is this bug.
lessons.comparisonNote: In Java you reach for threads: block a worker thread and only that thread parks — the UI thread and the pool carry on. In JavaScript there is exactly one thread running your code, so 'block' means *everything* stops: timers, input, rendering. Java's answer to slow work ('put it on another thread') becomes JavaScript's answer ('break it into tasks and yield to the loop' — the rendering lesson and the chunking exercise). Web Workers exist, but they're the exception you opt into, not the default the way a thread pool is in Java.
keyPoints: JS is single-threaded; the runtime owns the event loop. Your code runs on the call stack, one task at a time, run-to-completion.
Web APIs enqueue callbacks; they don't run them — `setTimeout(cb, 0)` still waits for the current task and everything queued ahead of it.
A long synchronous task freezes timers, input, and rendering — every main-thread jank bug is this bug.
Unbounded recursion overflows the fixed-size call stack: `RangeError`.

lessons.title: Microtasks vs Macrotasks: The Exact Ordering Rules
lessons.comparisonNote: Java has no equivalent of the microtask drain rule. `SwingUtilities.invokeLater` / `Platform.runLater` enqueue work onto the UI thread's event queue — that's the *macrotask* lane. But Java gives you no second, higher-priority lane that fully drains between tasks, and `CompletableFuture` callbacks run on pool threads with no cross-callback ordering guarantee. In JS the ordering is deterministic: learn the drain rule and you can trace any puzzle mechanically.
keyPoints: Two queues: macrotasks (`setTimeout`, I/O, events) and microtasks (promise reactions, `queueMicrotask`).
The drain rule: after each macrotask and whenever the stack empties, the *entire* microtask queue runs before the next macrotask.
Promise callbacks are never synchronous — even already-resolved promises defer to a microtask.
Microtasks queued during the drain extend it: long chains starve timers and rendering. Node's `process.nextTick` runs before promise microtasks (no browser equivalent).

lessons.title: Rendering Interplay: Where the Browser Paints
lessons.body:
# Rendering Interplay: Where the Browser Paints

The browser doesn't paint continuously — it paints *between* tasks. Miss where rendering slots into the loop and you'll misdiagnose every jank bug you'll ever meet.

## Paint happens between macrotasks

After the microtask drain and before the next macrotask, the browser may run the rendering steps: recalc styles, layout, paint, composite. Two consequences:

1. **Rendering never interrupts a task.** A 200ms synchronous loop means zero frames for 200ms — the page is frozen, not just slow.
2. **Rendering never happens mid-microtask-drain.** A long promise chain blocks paint exactly like a long task does. Microtasks are not "lighter" for rendering purposes.

```js
// This freezes the page for ~2s AND shows nothing until it's done:
button.addEventListener('click', () => {
  const start = performance.now();
  while (performance.now() - start < 2000) {} // never do this
  status.textContent = 'done'; // paints only after the handler returns
});
```

## Long tasks and INP

Chrome defines a **long task** as any main-thread task over 50ms. **INP (Interaction to Next Paint)** — the Core Web Vital that replaced FID — measures from user input to the next painted frame. A long task inside a click handler shows up directly in your INP score. "Keep handlers fast" is interview advice *and* production advice.

## Yielding strategies

When work is genuinely big, chunk it and yield so the browser can paint and handle input between chunks:

- `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0))` — yield to a macrotask; rendering and input get a turn.
- `scheduler.yield()` — the modern explicit "yield to the loop" (Chromium; progressive enhancement elsewhere).
- `requestIdleCallback` — for non-urgent work when the browser is idle.
- `requestAnimationFrame` — for work that must land before the next paint (visual updates).

Rule of thumb: keep tasks under 50ms; if a loop might exceed that, chunk it (that's your exercise).
lessons.comparisonNote: Java desktop developers already know this rule under a different name: *never block the Event Dispatch Thread.* Swing's EDT and JavaFX's application thread are single UI threads with exactly the same contract — long work goes to a `SwingWorker` / `Task`, and UI updates marshal back via `invokeLater` / `Platform.runLater`. The browser main thread is the web's EDT. The only difference is the yielding vocabulary: where Java hands work to another thread, JS chops work into tasks and yields to the loop.
keyPoints: The browser paints between macrotasks — never mid-task, never mid-microtask-drain.
A task over 50ms is a 'long task'; long tasks in input handlers directly hurt INP.
Yield with `setTimeout(0)`, `scheduler.yield()`, or `requestIdleCallback`; use `rAF` for visual updates.
Chunk any loop that might exceed ~50ms — responsiveness is a budget, not a feature.

lessons.title: Ordering Puzzles Dissected + Timer Gotchas
lessons.comparisonNote: Java's `ScheduledExecutorService.schedule(r, 0, MILLISECONDS)` runs on a pool thread promptly — 0 means 0, modulo thread availability. JavaScript's `setTimeout(fn, 0)` means 'no *additional* delay before enqueueing' — the callback still waits behind the entire queue, the microtask drain, and possibly rendering. In Java a zero delay is a deadline; in JS it's a place at the back of the line.
keyPoints: Trace puzzles by labeling each callback sync/micro/macro, then simulate: sync → drain microtasks → next macrotask.
`await` parks the function's continuation as a microtask — same rule, different syntax.
Browsers clamp deeply-nested `setTimeout` to 4ms+; `setInterval` skips rather than catches up — use recursive `setTimeout` for steady cadence.
Timer delays are minimums, not guarantees — never depend on timer precision for correctness.

exercises.title: Trace the order
exercises.prompt:
Predict the print order, then run the solution to check. Trace it with the drain rule before you look: which lines are sync, which queue a microtask, which queue a macrotask?

```js
console.log('A');
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C'));
console.log('D');
```

Expected solution output:
```
A
D
C
B
actual: A → D → C → B (sync first, then the microtask drain, then the timer)
```
hints: The script itself is a macrotask: it runs to completion (A, D) before any queued callback runs.
After the stack empties, the *entire* microtask queue drains before the next macrotask — so C beats B.
The summary line uses a 10ms `setTimeout` so it prints after the whole sequence.

exercises.title: Nested queues puzzle
hints: Sync first: 1, 6. The drain then runs the promise callback: 4, which queues a *second* timer.
Timer queue is now [timer-A, timer-B]. Timer-A prints 2 and queues a microtask — which drains before timer-B.
So the order is 1, 6, 4, 2, 3, 5. The summary uses a 10ms timer so it prints last.

exercises.title: Chunked processor
hints: The yield is one line: `await new Promise(res => setTimeout(res, 0))` — it parks the async function until a fresh macrotask.
The probe timer was queued *before* processing began, so it fires during your first yield — that's the proof the loop stayed alive.
Results must stay in input order: push per-item results sequentially, never reorder.

exercises.title: Starvation-proof drain
hints: In the naive drain, the probe timer is queued first but microtasks drain *before* the next macrotask — so all 1000 microtask hops run before the probe fires.
In the fair drain, after 250 items you `await` a timer; the timer queue is then [probe, resume] — the probe wins and sees `processed === 250`.
Skip the yield after the final batch (`i + 1 < items.length`) so the function resolves without a pointless extra macrotask.
